Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $x_0<\cdots<x_N$ be real nodes, let $y_0,\ldots,y_N\in\mathbb R$ be values, and let $m_0,\ldots,m_N\in\mathbb R$ be prescribed slopes. For $0\le i<N$ put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $t=(x-x_i)/h_i$ on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. Define
$$H_{00}(t)=2t^3-3t^2+1,\quad H_{01}(t)=-2t^3+3t^2,\quad H_{10}(t)=t^3-2t^2+t,\quad H_{11}(t)=t^3-t^2.$$
The cubic Hermite piece on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ is
$$P_i(x)=y_iH_{00}(t)+y_{i+1}H_{01}(t)+h_im_iH_{10}(t)+h_im_{i+1}H_{11}(t).$$
The piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant is the function whose restriction to each such interval is $P_i$; adjacent pieces use their common prescribed value $y_i$ at a shared node. The slopes $m_i$ are input data, not values inferred from neighboring pieces.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of

derivations.claim: By [F3], $f'$ is continuous. It cannot take both a positive and a negative value on $[a,b]$, since [F5] would then give a zero of $f'$, contradicting $|f'|\ge c$. Thus $f'$ has one sign throughout. On each grid cell [F4] gives $d_j=f'(\xi_j)$ for some interior $\xi_j$, so all secants have that sign and $|d_j|\ge c$. Admissibility of the grid gives $x_0<\cdots<x_N$, so $a<b$; [F8] makes $[a,b]$ compact. Since $f'$, $f''$, and $f'''$ are continuous by [F3], [F7] supplies $M_1,M_2,M_3\ge0$ with $|f'|\le M_1$, $|f''|\le M_2$, and $|f'''|\le M_3$ on $[a,b]$.

Fix an interior node $x_k$ and set $s=f'(x_k)$ and $q=f''(x_k)$. Applying [F6] with degree two at $x_k$ to $x_k-h$ and $x_k+h$ and dividing the remainders by $h$ gives $d_{k-1}=s-hq/2+e_-$ and $d_k=s+hq/2+e_+$, where $|e_-|,|e_+|\le M_3h^2/6$. Since $|s|\ge c$, for sufficiently small $h$ both secants stay bounded away from zero. The identity $1/(s+u)=1/s-u/s^2+u^2/(s^2(s+u))$ then gives, with a uniform constant, $1/d_{k-1}=1/s+hq/(2s^2)+O(h^2)$ and $1/d_k=1/s-hq/(2s^2)+O(h^2)$.

On a uniform grid the two weights in [F1] are both $3h$, so the interior slope equals $2/(1/d_{k-1}+1/d_k)$. The first-order terms in step 1.2 cancel, giving $1/d_{k-1}+1/d_k=2/s+O(h^2)$. Since $|s|\le M_1$, the leading term has magnitude at least $2/M_1$; thus the denominator stays bounded away from zero for sufficiently small $h$, and its reciprocal yields $m_k=s+O(h^2)$ with a constant uniform in $k$.

At the left endpoint, [F6] at $a$ gives $d_0=f'(a)+hf''(a)/2+O(M_3h^2)$ and $d_1=f'(a)+3hf''(a)/2+O(M_3h^2)$, by expanding $f(a+h)$ and $f(a+2h)$. Therefore the raw endpoint estimate in [F1] is $\widehat m_0=(3d_0-d_1)/2=f'(a)+O(M_3h^2)$. For small $h$ it has the sign of $f'(a)$; step 1.1 gives that same sign for $d_0,d_1$, so neither the sign clip nor the opposite-sign cap changes it. Reflecting the expansions at $b$ gives the identical $O(h^2)$ error for $m_N$.

The interior and endpoint estimates above use the bounds $M_1,M_2,M_3$ and $c^{-1}$ on the fixed interval; their constants and smallness thresholds are therefore uniform in the node index. Taking a common maximum for the error constants and a common positive minimum for the thresholds gives $C,h_0$ valid at every interior node and both endpoints. The finite list $|m_j-f'(x_j)|$, $0\le j\le N$, has a maximum by [F9], and the uniform pointwise estimate bounds it by $Ch^2$.

**Output:** Slopes $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ and the piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant determined by these nodes, values, and slopes under [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]].

Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$ for $0\le i<n-1$. Write $\operatorname{sgn}(r)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for the sign of a real number.

  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$

  $$\widehat m_0=\frac{(2h_0+h_1)d_0-h_0d_1}{h_0+h_1}.$$

  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $x_0<\cdots<x_N$ be real nodes, let $y_0,\ldots,y_N\in\mathbb R$ be values, and let $m_0,\ldots,m_N\in\mathbb R$ be prescribed slopes. For $0\le i<N$ put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $t=(x-x_i)/h_i$ on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. Define
$$H_{00}(t)=2t^3-3t^2+1,\quad H_{01}(t)=-2t^3+3t^2,\quad H_{10}(t)=t^3-2t^2+t,\quad H_{11}(t)=t^3-t^2.$$
The cubic Hermite piece on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ is
$$P_i(x)=y_iH_{00}(t)+y_{i+1}H_{01}(t)+h_im_iH_{10}(t)+h_im_{i+1}H_{11}(t).$$
The piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant is the function whose restriction to each such interval is $P_i$; adjacent pieces use their common prescribed value $y_i$ at a shared node. The slopes $m_i$ are input data, not values inferred from neighboring pieces.

For the data in [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]], each piece has the prescribed endpoint values and slopes: $P_i(x_i)=y_i$, $P_i(x_{i+1})=y_{i+1}$, $P_i'(x_i)=m_i$, and $P_i'(x_{i+1})=m_{i+1}$. The resulting interpolant is $C^1$ on $[x_0,x_N]$ (with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints). On a single interval, if the four prescribed endpoint data are the values and derivatives of a polynomial $q$ of degree at most three, then $P_i=q$ on that interval.

Let $f$ be $C^3$ on an open interval containing $[a,b]$, and suppose $|f'(x)|\ge c>0$ for every $x\in[a,b]$. For a uniform grid $x_j=a+jh$, $j=0,\ldots,N$, with $N\ge2$ and $h=(b-a)/N$, let $m_j$ be the slopes selected by [[alg-pchip-slope-selection]] from the values $f(x_j)$. There are constants $C,h_0>0$, depending on $f$, $c$, and $[a,b]$, such that for every such grid with $h<h_0$,
$$\max_{0\le j\le N}|m_j-f'(x_j)|\le Ch^2.$$

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

For $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, continuity at $x\in[a,b]$ means that for every
$\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $t\in[a,b]$ and $|t-x|<\delta$.
Differentiability at an interior point $c$ means that the two-sided limit
$$
f'(c)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}
$$
exists in the real field; differentiability on $(a,b)$ means this holds at
every interior point. For higher derivatives, define recursively
$f^{(j+1)}=(f^{(j)})'$ on the points where the derivative exists. The class
$C^{n+1}$ on an open interval means that these derivatives through order
$n+1$ exist and are continuous there.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $f$ is **bounded on $K$**: there is a real
$M \ge 0$ with

$$|f(x)| \le M \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, $f[K]$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-bounded-set]]).

**The hypothesis is compactness of $K$, not of $A$**, and it cannot be relaxed
to boundedness of $K$ or to closedness of $K$ alone: the identity is unbounded
on the closed set $[0,\infty)$, and $x \mapsto 1/x$ is unbounded on the bounded
set $(0,1)$. The general statement of that is
[[thm-compactness-is-necessary-for-evt-and-uniform-continuity]], later on this
page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

For real $x,y$, $|xy|=|x||y|$ and $|x+y|\le|x|+|y|$. For complex
$z,w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$, and if $w\ne0$ then
$|z/w|=|z|/|w|$.

derivations.claim: The admissible uniform grid has $x_0<\cdots<x_N$, so $a<b$ and $[a,b]$ is compact by [F9]. By [F7] and [F8], choose $M\ge0$ with $|f'''|\le M$ on $[a,b]$. Fix a cell $[x_i,x_i+h]$ and let $T_2$ be the degree-two Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $x_i$. By [F6], the residual $r=f-T_2$ satisfies $r(x_i)=r'(x_i)=0$, $|r(x_i+h)|\le Mh^3/6$, and $|r'(x_i+h)|\le Mh^2/2$; the derivative bound is [F6] applied to $f'$ with degree one.

Let $H$ be the exact-derivative Hermite piece for $f$ on this cell. The PCHIP piece $P_h$ and $H$ have identical endpoint values. By [F3], their difference is $h(m_i-f'(x_i))H_{10}(t)+h(m_{i+1}-f'(x_i+h))H_{11}(t)$. Since [F2] guarantees these PCHIP slopes are defined and $|H_{10}(t)|=t(1-t)^2\le1$, $|H_{11}(t)|\le1$, [F5] gives $|P_h(x)-H(x)|\le2C_sh^3$ for every $x$ in the cell.

For this exact-derivative Hermite piece $H$, linearity of the formula [F3] and reproduction [F4] give $H=T_2+H_r$, where $H_r(t)=r(x_i+h)H_{01}(t)+hr'(x_i+h)H_{11}(t)$. On $0\le t\le1$, $|H_{01}(t)|=t^2(3-2t)\le1$ and $|H_{11}(t)|=t^2(1-t)\le1$, so $|H_r(t)|\le(1/6+1/2)Mh^3=2Mh^3/3$. Together with $|r(x)|\le Mh^3/6$ from step 1.1, this yields $|H(x)-f(x)|\le5Mh^3/6$ for every $x$ in the cell.

Combining steps 2.1 and 1.2 gives $|P_h(x)-f(x)|\le(5M/6+2C_s)h^3$ for every $x\in[a,b]$, since the cells cover the interval. The constants do not depend on $i$ or $N$; put $C=5M/6+2C_s$. To justify the maximum in the statement, admissibility of the grid for [F1] gives $x_0<\cdots<x_N$, so $a<b$. By [F4], $P_h$ is $C^1$ and hence continuous on $[a,b]$; by [F7], $f$ is continuous there. Set $E(x)=|P_h(x)-f(x)|$. For $x,z\in[a,b]$, applying the triangle inequality twice gives $\bigl||P_h(x)-f(x)|-|P_h(z)-f(z)|\bigr|\le |(P_h(x)-f(x))-(P_h(z)-f(z))|\le |P_h(x)-P_h(z)|+|f(x)-f(z)|$, so $E$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. By [F9], $[a,b]$ is compact, and it is nonempty; [F10] therefore gives a point where $E$ attains its maximum. The pointwise bound just proved bounds that maximum by $Ch^3$.

For degree two, the cell polynomial is $c_{i,0}(1-t)^2+\iota\binom21\,c_{i,1}t(1-t)+c_{i,2}t^2$; this is the displayed Bernstein sum specialized to $n_i=2$.

Let $s\ge1$ be an integer and let $a=x_0<\cdots<x_s=b$ be a finite partition, and on each cell $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ choose an integer degree $n_i\ge0$ and real controls $c_{i,0},\ldots,c_{i,n_i}$. For $t=(x-x_i)/(x_{i+1}-x_i)\in[0,1]$, define the Bernstein basis polynomial
$$B_{k,n_i}(t)=\iota\binom{n_i}{k}t^k(1-t)^{n_i-k},\qquad 0\le k\le n_i,$$
where $\binom{n_i}{k}$ is the natural binomial coefficient from [[def-binomial-coefficient]], $\iota$ is the canonical embedding of [[def-canonical-natural]] into $\mathbb R$, and finite sums use [[def-finite-sum]]. The cell polynomial is $p_i(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n_i}c_{i,k}B_{k,n_i}(t)$. These cell polynomials form a piecewise Bernstein representation. To require continuity at a shared node, impose the additional endpoint-control condition $c_{i,n_i}=c_{i+1,0}$; continuity is not part of the representation unless that condition is imposed.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.

$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of [[lem-power-laws]]: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],
[[def-int-operations]]). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is

$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]),

injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every

citations.quote: Let $[a,b]$ be a bounded interval and let $a\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le b$ with $r\ge2$. A natural cubic spline with knots $t_1,\ldots,t_r$ is a $C^2$ function on $[a,b]$ that is a polynomial of degree at most three on every $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, has second derivative zero at $t_1$ and $t_r$, and is extended linearly on $[a,t_1]$ and $[t_r,b]$ when those intervals are nonempty. The knots $t_j$ are the distinct breakpoints; repeated observations at the same input do not create additional knots.

**Inputs:** An integer $n\ge2$, strictly increasing real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n-1}$, and real values $y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}$. All operations here are over the real numbers.

  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$

- For $n\ge3$, at the right endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$
  Apply the preceding clip and cap rule with $d_0,d_1$ replaced by $d_{n-2},d_{n-3}$ and $m_0,\widehat m_0$ replaced by $m_{n-1},\widehat m_{n-1}$.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.

If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.

If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

The shape theorem [F2] makes the first and last pieces monotone from $0$ to $1$ and from $1$ to $2$ and makes the middle piece constant. Thus the interpolant is globally nondecreasing, has no overshoot, and retains the flat interval exactly.

**Inputs:** An integer $n\ge2$, strictly increasing real nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n-1}$, and real values $y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}$. All operations here are over the real numbers.

**Output:** Slopes $m_0,\ldots,m_{n-1}$ and the piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant determined by these nodes, values, and slopes under [[def-piecewise-cubic-hermite-interpolant]].

Put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$ for $0\le i<n-1$. Write $\operatorname{sgn}(r)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for the sign of a real number.

- If $n=2$, set $m_0=m_1=d_0$.
- If $n\ge3$, for each interior node $1\le k\le n-2$, set $m_k=0$ when $d_{k-1}d_k\le0$. When $d_{k-1}d_k>0$, put $w_1=2h_k+h_{k-1}$, $w_2=h_k+2h_{k-1}$, and
  $$m_k=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{k-1}+w_2/d_k}.$$
- For $n\ge3$, at the left endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_0=\frac{(2h_0+h_1)d_0-h_0d_1}{h_0+h_1}.$$
  Set $m_0=0$ if $\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat m_0)\ne\operatorname{sgn}(d_0)$. Otherwise set $m_0=3d_0$ if $d_0d_1<0$ and $|\widehat m_0|>3|d_0|$; in all remaining cases set $m_0=\widehat m_0$.
- For $n\ge3$, at the right endpoint compute
  $$\widehat m_{n-1}=\frac{(2h_{n-2}+h_{n-3})d_{n-2}-h_{n-2}d_{n-3}}{h_{n-2}+h_{n-3}}.$$
  Apply the preceding clip and cap rule with $d_0,d_1$ replaced by $d_{n-2},d_{n-3}$ and $m_0,\widehat m_0$ replaced by $m_{n-1},\widehat m_{n-1}$.

For $n\ge3$, the algorithm returns the Hermite pieces from the stated values and selected slopes. The two-node branch is the line through the two input points.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, let $x_0<\cdots<x_N$ be real nodes, let $y_0,\ldots,y_N\in\mathbb R$ be values, and let $m_0,\ldots,m_N\in\mathbb R$ be prescribed slopes. For $0\le i<N$ put $h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $t=(x-x_i)/h_i$ on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$. Define
$$H_{00}(t)=2t^3-3t^2+1,\quad H_{01}(t)=-2t^3+3t^2,\quad H_{10}(t)=t^3-2t^2+t,\quad H_{11}(t)=t^3-t^2.$$
The cubic Hermite piece on $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ is
$$P_i(x)=y_iH_{00}(t)+y_{i+1}H_{01}(t)+h_im_iH_{10}(t)+h_im_{i+1}H_{11}(t).$$
The piecewise cubic Hermite interpolant is the function whose restriction to each such interval is $P_i$; adjacent pieces use their common prescribed value $y_i$ at a shared node. The slopes $m_i$ are input data, not values inferred from neighboring pieces.

Let $f$ be $C^3$ on an open interval containing $[a,b]$, with $|f'(x)|\ge c>0$ on $[a,b]$. On uniform grids $x_j=a+jh$, $j=0,\ldots,N$, $N\ge2$, let $P_h$ be the PCHIP interpolant to the values $f(x_j)$. There are constants $C,h_0>0$, depending only on $f$, $c$, and $[a,b]$, such that for every $h<h_0$,
$$\max_{x\in[a,b]}|P_h(x)-f(x)|\le Ch^3.$$
The assertion is limited to uniform grids and intervals on which the derivative stays bounded away from zero; it makes no third-order claim at an extremum.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

derivations.claim: The four secants are $d_0=-3h$, $d_1=-h$, $d_2=h$, and $d_3=3h$. At $x=-h$, the equal-width weights are $3h,3h$, so [F1] gives $m(-h)=6h/(3h/(-3h)+3h/(-h))=-3h/2$. At $x=0$ the adjacent secants have opposite signs, so [F1] gives $m(0)=0$.
With $t=(x+h)/h$ on $[-h,0]$, [F2] gives $P_h(x)/h^2=H_{00}(t)-\frac32H_{10}(t)=1-\frac32t+\frac12t^3$, whereas $f(x)/h^2=(1-t)^2$. Therefore $(P_h(x)-f(x))/h^2=\frac12t(1-t)^2$.

On this cell, step 2.1 gives the error $E(x)=|P_h(x)-f(x)|=\frac{h^2}{2}t(1-t)^2$, since $0\le t\le1$. This expression extends to a polynomial in $x$ through $t=(x+h)/h$, so [F4] makes it differentiable, hence continuous, on the cell. As $h>0$, the interval $[-h,0]$ is nonempty and compact by [F5]; [F6] therefore gives an attained maximum of $E$ there. Since $t=1/3$ corresponds to a point of the cell and step 2.1 gives $E=2h^2/27$ at that point, the maximum is at least $2h^2/27$. A uniform bound $|P_h-f|\le Ch^3$ on cells adjacent to this extremum would then imply $2/27\le Ch$ for every sufficiently small $h$, which is impossible as $h\to0$. The hypothesis $|f'|\ge c>0$ in [F3] also fails because [F4] gives $f'(0)=0$.
